strings.tab141.p1: Comparing the theoretical with the experimental values we find that the caloric equations of state, derived for the ideal monatomic and diatomic gas respectively, hold to a good approximation for real gases as well. strings.tr.izobar.lead: The pressure stays constant, so the gas does mechanical work while expanding.

strings.tr.izoterm.title: Isothermal transformation · T = constant
strings.tr.izoterm.lead: The temperature is constant, so the internal energy of an ideal gas does not change.
strings.izo.p1: By the first law, all the heat exchanged with the outside becomes mechanical work. With the equation of state and p = νRT/V we get:
strings.izo.p2: The graph is a hyperbola. The magnitude of work is the area under the curve: L > 0 during expansion and L < 0 during compression. The demonstration uses T = 300 K and minimum volume 10 L.

strings.tr.adiabat.title: Adiabatic transformation · Q = 0
strings.tr.adiabat.lead: In an adiabatic change, by definition, the gas exchanges no heat with its surroundings.
strings.ad.p1: Using the thermal equation of state, the adiabatic relation can be rewritten as:
strings.ad.p2: And the adiabatic work takes three equivalent forms:
strings.ad.p3: Then, by the first law (Q = 0), the change in internal energy is ΔU = ν·C_V·(T_f − T_i) = m·c_V·(T_f − T_i).
strings.ad.obs.title: Observations
strings.ad.obs1: The equation of the adiabatic transformation was obtained in 1823 by Siméon-Denis Poisson.
strings.ad.obs2: The adiabatic exponent is greater than one: γ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas and γ = 7/5 for a diatomic one.
strings.ad.obs3: Because γ > 1, in an adiabatic process the pressure varies with volume faster than in the isothermal one. That is why the adiabat is steeper than the isotherm and an adiabat and an isotherm intersect at a single point.

strings.synth.heat.p: The heat absorbed by the gas always splits in two: internal energy (which for an ideal gas depends only on temperature) and mechanical work. The splitting ratio is precisely γ.

strings.ex141.title: Isobaric heating of 2 kg of oxygen
strings.ex141.text: Heating 2 kg of oxygen isobarically by ΔT = 5 K requires supplying the gas with Q = 9.16 kJ of heat. Find: a) the isobaric specific heat c<sub>p</sub> of oxygen; b) the mechanical work L done by the gas during the isobaric expansion; c) the change ΔU of its internal energy.
strings.ex142.title: Heating oxygen in a constant-volume vessel
strings.ex142.text: A vessel of constant volume holds m = 1 g of oxygen with isochoric specific heat c<sub>V</sub> = 700 J/(kg·K), at t = 27 °C and pressure p₁ = 100 kPa. Find the heat Q needed to raise its pressure to p₂ = 200 kPa.
strings.ex143.title: Derive the two Poisson relations and the adiabatic work
strings.ex143.text: Derive the two relations above (T·V<sup>γ−1</sup> = constant and T·p<sup>(1−γ)/γ</sup> = constant). Using the adiabatic equation one can then show the expression for the mechanical work.
strings.ex144.title: Mechanical work in an adiabatic expansion
strings.ex144.text: Find the mechanical work L done by the ideal gas in an adiabatic transformation from pressure p₁ between volumes V₁ and V₂. The adiabatic coefficient γ is given. Application: p₁ = 1 bar; V₁ = 10 cm³; V₂ = 20 cm³; γ = 1.4.
strings.ex145.title: Vertical pump with a piston — integrative problem
strings.ex145.text: A vertical pump barrel of cross-section S, fitted with a movable piston of mass M, contains nitrogen of mass m at temperature t₁. The atmospheric pressure is p<sub>a</sub>. The gas undergoes isobaric heating up to T₂, after which the piston is locked and the barrel is connected to a vessel of volume V₂. Find: a) the initial height h of the piston above the barrel base; b) the work L done by the gas during the isobaric heating; c) the final pressure p<sub>f</sub> after the connection is opened.
strings.ex145.data: Application: S = 0.01 m²; M = 50 kg; m = 14 g; t₁ = 27 °C; p_a = 1 bar; T₂ = 400 K; V₂ = 3 dm³; p₂ = 4·10⁵ Pa; g = 10 m/s².
strings.ex1411.title: The linear process in (p, V) coordinates
strings.ex1411.text: For a fixed amount of ideal gas following the linear process p = kV, find the polytropic index n, the molar heat capacity C and the work L between temperatures T_i and T_f.

strings.cal.degrees.mono: 3 translations = 3 degrees of freedom. The atom can move independently along Ox, Oy and Oz. The monatomic model includes no internal rotations or vibrations.
strings.cal.degrees.di: 3 translations + 2 rotations = 5 degrees of freedom. Initially, the bond is aligned with Ox. The Oy and Oz controls rotate the molecule relative to the fixed frame; a linear molecule has two orientational degrees of freedom. Rotation about the bond and vibrations are excluded in this rigid model.
strings.cal.degrees.poly: 3 translations + 3 rotations = 6 degrees of freedom. This example is a rigid nonlinear molecule, with three independent rotational axes. A linear polyatomic molecule has only two relevant rotations. Vibrations are excluded.

text.q: In an isochoric transformation of an ideal gas, which quantity is zero?
opts: The change of internal energy ΔU
text.why: ΔV = 0 ⇒ L_if = 0, so all of Q_if becomes ΔU.

text.q: What is the molar heat at constant volume C_V of a monatomic gas? (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))
Which is the correct statement of Robert Mayer’s relation?
text.why: C_p = C_V + R; hence C_p = (5/2)R for a monatomic gas.

text.q: For a diatomic gas, the adiabatic exponent γ equals:
Oxygen: m = 2 kg, ΔT = 5 K, Q = 9.16 kJ at constant pressure. What is the isobaric specific heat c_p?
In the problem above, what is ΔU if L = 2.598 kJ?
Which expression for the mechanical work belongs to the isothermal change?
text.why: At constant T, p = νRT/V and the integral yields the natural logarithm of the volume ratio.

text.q: Rigid vessel: m = 1 g oxygen, c_V = 700 J/(kg·K), T₁ = 300.15 K, p₁ = 100 kPa → p₂ = 200 kPa. What is the correct heat Q?
Why is the adiabat steeper than the isotherm in (p, V) coordinates?
opts: Because γ > 1, so pressure varies faster with V
text.why: p ∝ V^(−γ) versus p ∝ V^(−1); since γ > 1 the adiabat drops faster and the two curves meet at a single point.

text.q: Which correspondence is correct for the adiabatic transformation?
Adiabatic expansion: p₁ = 1 bar, V₁ = 10 cm³ → V₂ = 20 cm³, γ = 1.4. What is the work L?
In a polytropic process pVⁿ = constant, which simple process corresponds to n → ∞?
text.why: n = 0 ⇒ isobaric, n = 1 ⇒ isothermal, n = γ ⇒ adiabatic, n → ∞ ⇒ isochoric.

text.q: From n = (C − C_p)/(C − C_V), what does n = γ mean for the molar heat C of the process?
text.why: With C = 0, n = (0 − C_p)/(0 − C_V) = C_p/C_V = γ: the adiabat is the polytrope whose molar heat vanishes.

answers.ex143: T·V^(γ−1) = ct,  T·p^((1−γ)/γ) = ct,  L_if = −νC_V(T_f − T_i)

temperatures: At %T K we use the rigid diatomic model: 3 translations + 2 rotations, i = 5. Its precise range of validity depends on the gas.
At %T K vibrations may become important, depending on the gas. There is no universal threshold at 600 K; C_V and γ then vary with temperature.
At %T K some rotations may be weakly excited, depending on the gas. The thresholds are molecule-specific; the classical i = 5 model may not apply.
